title: Moderate bilateral SNHL with a quiet family communication goal

patient.chiefConcern: Difficulty following small-group family conversations during meals

featurePrompt: Which features should drive rehabilitation planning?

keyFeatures.label: Primary setting
keyFeatures.value: Small family meals and quiet home conversations

keyFeatures.label: Patient goal
keyFeatures.value: Follow family conversation with less repetition

summary: This case is designed to test person-centred rehabilitation: the same general hearing-loss profile can lead to a different plan when the patient's listening environments and goals change.

stages.title: 1. Identify the functional problem
stages.prompt: What should anchor the rehabilitation plan?

options.text: The patient's difficulty following family conversations during meals
The audiogram alone, without asking about communication situations
A generic device recommendation before identifying goals

stages.feedback: The functional communication problem is the starting point for person-centred rehabilitation.

stages.title: 2. Interpret the hearing profile
stages.prompt: How should the bilateral sloping loss be used in planning?

options.text: Use it together with the patient's communication needs, preferences and listening environment
Treat the degree of loss as the only determinant of rehabilitation
Ignore the audiogram once the patient reports difficulty

stages.feedback: Audiometric findings inform the plan, but they do not replace functional needs assessment.

stages.title: 3. Screen for barriers and safety needs
stages.prompt: Which approach is most appropriate before selecting interventions?

options.text: Check communication barriers, dexterity, motivation and relevant safety needs
Assume all older adults have identical rehabilitation barriers
Skip contextual questions because the hearing loss is already measured

stages.feedback: A rehabilitation plan should account for patient-specific barriers and practical factors.

stages.title: 4. Select the rehabilitation plan
stages.prompt: Which plan best fits this patient's stated goal?

options.text: Individualized hearing-aid use plus communication strategies and family-partner education for meals
Advanced technology chosen solely because it is available
No intervention until the patient reports complete communication failure

stages.feedback: The plan should match the patient's real-world goal and include communication strategies, not just technology.

stages.title: 5. Justify the plan
stages.prompt: What is the strongest rationale?

options.text: The intervention is matched to the patient's priority communication situation and can be reviewed using functional outcomes
A more expensive device is automatically more person-centred
Audiometric severity proves which lifestyle goals matter

stages.feedback: The rationale should explicitly connect patient goals to the selected intervention.

stages.title: 6. Plan outcome measurement
stages.prompt: How should progress be evaluated?

options.text: Review the patient's functional communication goal and adjust the plan based on reported outcomes
Only repeat pure-tone thresholds
Close the case after device delivery

stages.feedback: Outcome-focused follow-up links management back to the patient's stated communication goal.

title: Moderate bilateral SNHL with meetings and lectures

patient.chiefConcern: Difficulty understanding speech in noisy corporate boardrooms and lectures

featurePrompt: Which features make this rehabilitation plan different from a quiet family setting?

keyFeatures.label: Context
keyFeatures.value: Active professional and frequent group communication

summary: B2 intentionally uses a similar audiometric profile to B1 but a different lifestyle demand, testing whether management is individualized rather than audiogram-driven.

stages.title: 1. Identify the functional problem
stages.prompt: Which need should lead the rehabilitation formulation?

options.text: Speech understanding in noisy meetings and lectures
Only the patient's threshold average
Cosmetic appearance of the device

stages.feedback: The high-demand listening environment is central to the rehabilitation goal.

stages.title: 2. Interpret the hearing profile
stages.prompt: What does the profile tell you when combined with the listening goal?

options.text: The hearing loss contributes to the difficulty, but the management plan must also address speech-in-noise demands
The audiogram completely determines the technology choice
Noise management is unrelated to hearing rehabilitation

stages.feedback: Audiometry and listening environment should be integrated rather than considered separately.

stages.title: 3. Screen for practical barriers
stages.prompt: What should be checked before finalizing the plan?

options.text: Technology comfort, communication demands, assistive options and realistic expectations
Whether the patient can tolerate silence only
No additional factors because the loss is bilateral

stages.feedback: High-demand rehabilitation requires attention to usability and expectations as well as hearing findings.

stages.title: 4. Select the rehabilitation plan
stages.prompt: Which plan best matches the patient's environment?

options.text: Appropriately fitted hearing aids with speech-in-noise strategies and consideration of a remote microphone/assistive option
Use the simplest plan regardless of meeting demands
Recommend avoiding meetings

stages.feedback: The plan should directly address communication in noise and the patient's active professional role.

stages.title: 5. Justify the plan
stages.prompt: Which justification best demonstrates individualized reasoning?

options.text: The selected features and strategies are linked to the patient's real-world speech-in-noise goals
The most advanced feature is always the correct choice
All moderate losses require the same rehabilitation package

stages.feedback: The rationale should link intervention choices to the specific listening context.

stages.title: 6. Plan outcome measurement
stages.prompt: What should be reviewed at follow-up?

options.text: Speech-in-noise function, meeting participation, device use and patient-reported benefit
Only whether the device turns on
Only unaided thresholds

stages.feedback: Follow-up should measure the functional outcomes that motivated rehabilitation.

title: Moderate bilateral SNHL with limited dexterity and remote-family communication

patient.chiefConcern: Difficulty communicating with children by telephone while living alone

featurePrompt: Which patient factors should shape the rehabilitation design?

keyFeatures.label: Goal
keyFeatures.value: Clearer calls with children and reliable access to alerts

keyFeatures.label: Barrier
keyFeatures.value: Limited hand dexterity affects device handling

summary: B3 emphasizes usability, connectivity and independent living. The intervention should be practical for the patient's motor abilities and communication routine.

stages.title: 1. Identify the functional problem
stages.prompt: What should be prioritized?

options.text: Telephone clarity and independent access to important communication or alerts
Only the audiometric configuration
Aesthetic preference before functional needs

stages.feedback: The patient's independence and telephone communication goal should anchor the rehabilitation plan.

stages.title: 2. Interpret the hearing and usability profile
stages.prompt: What additional factor changes the rehabilitation approach?

options.text: Limited dexterity may affect handling, controls and daily device management
Dexterity has no relevance to rehabilitation
Only visual acuity matters

stages.feedback: Usability is a clinical consideration when independent device handling is part of the patient's routine.

stages.title: 3. Screen for barriers and safety
stages.prompt: What should be explored?

options.text: Dexterity, telephone access, emergency-alert needs, support network and realistic device-management ability
Assume a family member will manage everything
Ignore emergency communication because it is not an audiogram variable

stages.feedback: The case explicitly requires attention to independent living and practical support.

stages.title: 4. Select the rehabilitation plan
stages.prompt: Which plan best matches the goal and barrier?

options.text: Usable hearing technology with telephone/streaming support, simplified controls and appropriate caregiver or family training
Choose the device with the greatest number of manual controls
Avoid technology because dexterity is limited

stages.feedback: The intervention should reduce handling burden while supporting communication and independence.

stages.title: 5. Justify the plan
stages.prompt: Which rationale is strongest?

options.text: The plan matches communication goals while adapting the technology and training to the patient's dexterity
Family members should make all decisions
Usability is separate from clinical rehabilitation

stages.feedback: Person-centred care includes adapting the intervention to the patient's practical abilities.

stages.title: 6. Plan outcome measurement
stages.prompt: What should follow-up assess?

options.text: Telephone success, device handling, independence and patient-reported benefit
Only device appearance
Only aided thresholds

stages.feedback: Follow-up should test whether the intervention actually improves the patient's functional goal.

title: Low readiness for change with high family pressure

patient.chiefConcern: Family reports communication difficulty, but the patient is not ready to use hearing technology

featurePrompt: What is the central rehabilitation issue beyond the hearing loss itself?

keyFeatures.label: Social context
keyFeatures.value: Strong family pressure to obtain a device

summary: B4 tests readiness-sensitive counselling. The educational goal is to avoid coercive device recommendations and build a collaborative rehabilitation plan.

stages.title: 1. Identify the rehabilitation problem
stages.prompt: What should be explored first?

options.text: The patient's own goals, concerns and readiness for change
The family's preferred device model
Immediate fitting without discussing readiness

stages.feedback: The patient's perspective and readiness are essential to shared decision-making.

stages.title: 2. Interpret the profile
stages.prompt: How should the hearing findings be used?

options.text: Use them to explain the communication problem and possible options without turning them into a forced prescription
Use the thresholds to override patient preference
Ignore the findings completely

stages.feedback: Clinical information should support informed choice rather than replace it.

stages.title: 3. Screen for readiness and pressure
stages.prompt: Which factor is especially important here?

options.text: Low readiness and family pressure may affect engagement, so coercion should be avoided
Family pressure guarantees good adherence
Readiness is unrelated to rehabilitation outcomes

stages.feedback: Readiness and autonomy are central to a sustainable rehabilitation plan.

stages.title: 4. Select the rehabilitation approach
stages.prompt: What is the most person-centred next step?

options.text: Use motivational and counselling strategies, clarify goals, involve communication partners appropriately and allow the patient to participate in timing the intervention
Pressure the patient to accept a device because family members are concerned
Discharge without discussing any options

stages.feedback: The protocol specifically highlights readiness-sensitive counselling and shared decision-making.

stages.title: 5. Justify the approach
stages.prompt: Which rationale is most defensible?

options.text: Autonomy and readiness are addressed while keeping rehabilitation options open and linked to the patient's goals
A clinician should decide what the patient needs regardless of readiness
Family preference is equivalent to patient preference

stages.feedback: The rationale should show respect for patient autonomy while maintaining a pathway to future rehabilitation.

stages.title: 6. Plan follow-up
stages.prompt: What would be useful after the counselling session?

options.text: Revisit goals and readiness later, with patient-chosen communication strategies and appropriate family involvement
Require an immediate device decision
End all future contact

stages.feedback: Readiness can change; follow-up should preserve an accessible path back to rehabilitation.
